title: The Cairo Geniza
hookLine: a storeroom where worn writings were kept, holding centuries of daily life

lines: A SHOPPING LIST, A CHILD'S ALPHABET.
A ROOM IN A CAIRO SYNAGOGUE.
YOU DON'T THROW IT IN THE TRASH.
cards: A shopping list. A child's alphabet practice, the letters wobbling across the page. A marriage contract.
A merchant's letter complaining about a late ship. A page of poetry. A page of the Torah, worn soft.
All of it in one dark room high in the wall of a synagogue in old Cairo, the Ben Ezra synagogue. Nobody meant it as an archive.
People put papers there for one reason: they had God's name on them, or holy words, or Hebrew letters, and you don't throw that in the trash. So for centuries, the paper piled up.

teach.h: A STOREROOM FOR WORN HOLY WRITINGS.
teach.b: A geniza is a storeroom for worn-out holy writings.
The idea is already in the Mishnah: in tractate Shabbat it says holy writings may be rescued from a fire, and that those which can't be read from are to be stored away.
The Hebrew for that storing away is the same word, geniza. The custom grows from respect.

A book with God's name in it is not just paper, so when a prayer book falls apart or a Torah scroll can no longer be read, it isn't thrown away. It's stored, and in time it may be buried, the way a person is.
In Cairo, the pages stayed in the room, and the dry air seems to have kept them.

Because people there seem to have put almost anything with Hebrew letters inside, the room ended up holding ordinary life: business letters, court records, recipes, prescriptions, love poems, and the handwriting of children learning to read.
When scholars finally carried the papers out and began to read them, a world came back: merchants trading across seas, women in court over property, families writing to sons far away.
That's the reason any of this survived: nothing holy thrown away. A habit of respect for words became, without anyone planning it, a memory for a whole community.

how: Synagogues and Jewish homes set aside worn prayer books, Bibles and other pages with God's name, and communities later bury them in a Jewish cemetery rather than throwing them away.

games.q: you're in old Cairo. a prayer book has fallen apart, and its pages carry God's name. what do you do with it?
games.why: it goes into the geniza. because people put almost anything with Hebrew letters there, the Cairo Geniza ended up holding a whole world.

practice: Bring to mind a paper in your life that carries someone: a card in a drawer, a note in a parent's handwriting, a message from someone who's gone, a child's drawing.
Hold it in your mind and ask why you've kept it, or why you might; ordinary words become precious when someone wrote them. If you pray, you can remember the person whose hand is on it.
